problem: Embodied navigation research communicates goals almost only through natural-language instructions. Nonverbal cues such as gestures are unexplored, and prior gesture-based HRI relies on predefined gesture vocabularies with fixed meanings.
motivation: Gestures are immediate and intuitive, and can say "go there" more succinctly than a long sentence, especially when human and agent share a scene. Human gestures are diverse and context-dependent, so the agent should learn their semantics from the navigation task itself rather than from predefined gestures.
key_idea: Put a human in the same simulated scene and let them guide an ObjectGoal agent with free-form, unlabeled natural gestures (recorded body and hand poses). The agent learns end-to-end with PPO to interpret the gestures, so learning gesture semantics and learning navigation help each other.
insight: Gesture semantics can be learned from the navigation reward alone, with no predefined gesture meanings. Adding gesture input to the vision-plus-category baseline raises SR in most scene types. Intervention (rejective) gestures help far more than referencing gestures (avg test SR 23.8 vs 13.0), presumably because they are a direct, low-ambiguity directional signal. Referencing gestures do not help in living rooms (SR falls below the baseline), and the gain is not uniform across scene types.
method: GesTHOR environment: a Unity/AI2-THOR (iTHOR) VR framework with Oculus Rift, Kinect v2 and Leap Motion. A human in the same scene sees the target and gestures. The learning side is in PyTorch (AllenAct) and connects to Unity through an external communicator.

Gesture dataset: pre-recorded gestures stand in for real-time interaction. There are 230k+ training episodes and 2,500 validation/test episodes of free-form referencing gestures from volunteers with no prescribed gestures. There are also 10 recorded rejective intervention gestures.

Gesture input: each gesture is a 100-step sequence of 95 features (Unity humanoid muscle values for body and hands). Referencing gestures come from the episode. Intervention gestures are sampled at random and shown only when the agent's heading is more than 90° away from the target.

Model: a frozen ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 encodes RGB and depth (only the last FC layer is trained). A flattened gesture vector is encoded, and the target category goes through an embedding. An observation combiner concatenates all features, followed by a GRU and an actor-critic head.

PPO training: rewards are +1 for success, -0.001 per step, -0.005 per collision (to discourage sliding) and -0.01 for a stop in an ineligible location. Settings: horizon 128, batch 128, 4 epochs, Adam with lr 3e-4, gamma 0.99. Actions are move forward 0.25 m, turn left/right 15°, and stop.

Evaluation protocol: separate models per room type (kitchen, living room, bedroom, bathroom), with 20/5/5 train/val/test scenes each. Success requires a stop within 1.5 m with the target visible, and episodes are capped at 100 steps. SR and SPL are reported for 1, 2, 3 or unlimited stops.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 (ImageNet-pretrained, frozen except last FC) + gesture encoder + GRU actor-critic, trained with PPO
setting.training_data: RL in GesTHOR on AI2-THOR iTHOR scenes (20 train rooms per type), with 230k+ pre-recorded human gesture episodes
setting.observation: egocentric RGB + depth (224x224), target category label, collision signal, human gesture pose sequence (100x95)
setting.action_space: low-level: move forward 0.25 m, turn left/right 15°, stop
setting.privileged: Human gesture cues (recorded while the human sees the target) and the target category label. Intervention gestures use ground-truth agent-target heading (>90°).

numbers_note: The custom GesTHOR benchmark is not a standard one. Table 1 averages are inconsistent with Table 2 (e.g. Intervention test SPL 16.1 appears as the validation SPL of 26.3 in Table 1 and as the 1-stop SR of 26.3 in Table 2), so the Average rows may be mislabeled. Only test results are listed.
results: With gestures, the average first-stop test SR is 23.8 (intervention) and 13.0 (referencing) versus 9.9 for the vision-only baseline, and above Scene Prior (13.4, which uses scene priors rather than gestures). With unlimited stops, intervention reaches an average SR of 68.7 versus 40.4 for the baseline. Referencing gestures are not uniformly helpful (living room SR drops from 3.5 to 2.7).
limitations: Gestures are pre-recorded and replayed rather than truly interactive, and the target category is given as a label, so it is not full multimodal target inference.
Absolute success rates are low (first-stop SR under 25% on average), and the test scenes and tasks are limited (4 room types, 38 categories, separate models per room type).
Table 1 and Table 2 average rows are inconsistent, and there is no comparison with language-instruction agents.
